title: Electric Current and Current Density
short_intro: Electric current is defined as the rate of flow of net electric charge through a given cross-section of a conductor. Microscopic analysis relates macroscopic current to the drift velocity of free charge carriers within the conductor lattice.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of electric current, Ohm's law, resistance, resistivity, grouping of resistors, and simple DC circuits.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Drift velocity derivation, microscopic form of Ohm's law (J = σE), temperature dependence of resistivity, and complex network analysis using Kirchhoff's laws.

prerequisites: Electrostatic potential and electric field inside conductors
Basic vector calculus and scalar product

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Nature of Electric Current
bullets: Electric current is a scalar quantity defined as the rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt.
The SI unit of electric current is the Ampere (A), which is a fundamental SI unit equal to one Coulomb per second.
Even though it has magnitude and direction, current does not obey the parallelogram law of vector addition, hence it is classified as a scalar.

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Model and Drift Velocity
bullets: Free electrons in a conductor move randomly with thermal velocities of the order of 10&sup5; m/s.
When an electric field E is applied, electrons acquire a small net directed velocity opposite to the field, known as drift velocity (v&subscript;d).
Drift velocity is typically of the order of 10&sup-&sup4; m/s, which is extremely small compared to thermal velocity or the speed of propagation of the electric field.

concept_notes.heading: Current Density and Vector Form of Ohm's Law
bullets: Current density (J) is a vector quantity defined as current per unit cross-sectional area normal to the direction of flow: J = I/A = ne v&subscript;d.
The SI unit of current density is Ampere per square meter (A/m²).
The microscopic form of Ohm's law relates current density to the electric field via conductivity (σ): J = σE.

concept_notes.heading: Mobility of Charge Carriers
bullets: Mobility (μ) is defined as the magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field: μ = v&subscript;d / E.
The SI unit of mobility is m²/(V·s).
Conductivity can be expressed in terms of carrier concentration (n), charge of electron (e), and mobility (μ) as σ = neμ.

derivations.title: Relation between Electric Current and Drift Velocity
derivations.conditions: Uniform conductor of cross-sectional area A, uniform free electron density n, and uniform drift velocity v&subscript;d.
steps: Consider a cylinder of length v&subscript;d dt inside a conductor through which electrons drift in time dt.
The volume of this cylinder is A v&subscript;d dt, and the number of free electrons contained in it is N = n A v&subscript;d dt.
The total charge contained in this volume is dQ = N e = n e A v&subscript;d dt.
The current is given by I = dQ / dt = n e A v&subscript;d.

derivations.title: Derivation of Microscopic Ohm's Law from Drude Model
derivations.conditions: Conductor under steady electric field E, relaxation time τ.
$steps: The acceleration of an electron in an electric field E is given by a = e E / m, where m is the mass of the electron.
Drift velocity is the average velocity attained between collisions, given by v_d = a τ = (e E / m) τ.
Substitute v_d into the current density relation J = n e v_d to get J = n e (e E / m) τ = (ne^2τ / m) E.
Identify conductivity σ = ne^2τ / m, yielding vector form J = σE.

graphs_and_experiments.title: V-I Characteristic Graph for Metallic Conductor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a V (voltage) versus I (current) plot at constant temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the V-I graph (dV/di) represents the electrical resistance R of the conductor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT to identify ohmic devices and calculate resistance from graphical slopes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resistivity vs Temperature for Metals
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve that starts near zero at absolute zero and increases almost linearly at higher temperatures, curving slightly at lower temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that resistance increases with temperature due to increased frequency of atomic collisions reducing relaxation time.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing between metallic conductors and semiconductors (which show negative temperature coefficient).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Meter Bridge Experiment (Verification of Laws of Resistance)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing a 1-meter resistance wire, resistance box, unknown resistor, galvanometer, and jockey.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Based on Wheatstone bridge principle at balance point: R/S = l_1 / (100 - l_1).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Testing experimental determination of unknown resistance and specific resistance.

solved_numericals.question: A current of 2 A flows through a uniform wire of cross-sectional area 1 mm^2. If the free electron density in the wire is 10^28 m^-3, calculate the drift velocity of the electrons.
solution_steps: Identify given values: I = 2 A, A = 1 mm^2 = 10^-6 m^2, n = 10^28 m^-3, e = 1.6 \times 10^-19 C.
Use the formula for current: I = neAv_d.
Rearrange to solve for drift velocity: v_d = I / (neA).

solved_numericals.question: An aluminum wire of diameter 2 mm and length 3 m is connected across a potential difference of 2 V. If the resistivity of aluminum is 2.8 \times 10^-8 \Omega\cdot\text{m}, find the current density inside the wire.
solution_steps: Calculate radius r = d / 2 = 1 mm = 10^-3 m.
Calculate cross-sectional area A = \pi r^2 = \pi (10^-3)^2 = \pi \times 10^-6 m^2.
Calculate current I = V / R = 2 / R.
Calculate current density J = I / A = V / (R A) = V / (\rho l) = 2 / (2.8 \times 10^-8 \times 3).

solved_numericals.question: The resistance of a metallic wire at 20 \deg\text{C} is 20 \Omega. If the temperature coefficient of resistance is 0.004 /\deg\text{C}, at what temperature will the resistance become 40 \Omega?

assumptions_and_limitations: Ohm's law assumes that physical conditions such as temperature and mechanical strain remain constant during current flow.
The Drude model assumes classical mechanics apply to electrons, treating them as an ideal gas colliding with fixed heavy ions, which fails at very low temperatures where quantum effects dominate.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electric current flows at the speed of light inside a conductor.
common_misconceptions.correct: The electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light, but the actual drift velocity of electrons is extremely small (order of 10^-4 m/s).
common_misconceptions.why: Electrons undergo continuous random collisions and drift slowly under the electric field.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Current is a vector quantity because it has both magnitude and direction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Current is a scalar quantity because it does not follow the vector addition laws (parallelogram law).
common_misconceptions.why: The sum of currents at a junction depends only on algebraic addition (Kirchhoff's Current Law).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Resistance depends on the applied potential difference and current.
common_misconceptions.correct: Resistance is an intrinsic property of the conductor geometry and material (R = \rho l / A), independent of V and I for ohmic conductors.
common_misconceptions.why: Ratio V/I remains constant for ohmic materials irrespective of individual changes in V or I.

quick_revision: Current is the scalar rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt.
Vector form of Ohm's law: J = \sigma E.
Drift velocity is directly proportional to the applied electric field: v_d = \mu E.
Resistance varies with temperature according to R_T = R_0 [1 + \alpha \Delta T].
